Copper-catalyzed 1,4-alkylcyanation of
CF -containing 1,3-enynes: alkoxy radical-mediated
selective cleavage of fused azabicycles
Jun-Lin Lu, Hong-Fei Liu, Ying-Xin Shui, Qi-Chao Shan, Xin-Hua Duan * and
Li-Na Guo *
rsc.li/chemcomm
A copper-catalyzed 1,4-alkylcyanation of
\mathsf { C F } _ { 3 } .
-containing 1,3-enynes
with bicyclic hydroperoxides and TMSCN is described. In this cascade,
the alkyl source originates from selective cleavage of a C–C bond in
the fused bicyclic skeletons, enabling the successful introduction of a
succinimide fragment into tetrasubstituted allenes. This reaction is
characterized by mild conditions, broad substrate scope, excellent
functional group tolerance, and ease of large-scale synthesis and
product derivatization.

ing indicated that THF also afforded a satisfactory yield of 3aa, yet
DCE remained the optimal solvent (entries 7–10). Sequentially,
various bidentate and tridentate nitrogen ligands, including

Then, the generality and limitations of 1,3-enynes were
investigated using 1a as the alkylation reagent (Scheme 3).
1,3-Enynes bearing aryl, heteroaryl and alkyl substituents in
the alkyne moiety reacted eficiently with 1a and TMSCN,
furnishing the desired products 3ab–3an in good yields. Both
electronic and steric effects of substituents on the aromatic ring
did not show a significant impact on the reaction efficiency.
Additionally, synthetically useful functional groups such as ester
(3ae), cyano (3af) and bromo (3ah) were all compatible with this
catalytic system. When the trifluoromethyl group on the 1,3-enyne
was replaced by a hydrogen atom, a methyl group and a methyl
ester group, the corresponding products 3ao, 3ap and 3aq were
successfully obtained, but with noticeably reduced yields. This
decrease in yield might be due to a polarity mismatch. The alkyl
radicals generated by the carbon–carbon bond cleavage are
nucleophilic, and thus, electron-deficient

Based on the above experimental results and literature,<sup>11–13</sup>
a possible reaction mechanism was proposed. As shown in
Scheme
the reaction begins with the single-electron
reduction of the fused bicyclic hydroperoxide 1a by the Cu(I)
complex I formed in situ, yielding the radical intermediate III
and the Cu(II) species II. Subsequently, the alkoxy radical III
undergoes a selective b-scission to give the ring-opening, rela-
tively stable alkyl radical IV. Intermediate IV is captured by the
CF -1,3-enyne 2a to form a propargyl radical species V, which
resonates to produce the allenyl radical VI. Meanwhile, the
Cu(II) species II undergoes a ligand exchange with TMSCN to
yield the key intermediate VII. The interaction of intermediates
VI and VII forms a Cu(III) species VIII. Finally, reductive
elimination of Cu(III) species VIII gives the target product 3aa
and regenerates the Cu(I) complex I. Fortunately, all relevant
copper complexes can be detected by HRMS.

In summary, we have developed a copper-catalyzed 1,4-
alkylcyanation of 1,3-enynes with bicyclic hydroperoxides and
TMSCN. In this cascade, the bicyclic hydroperoxides serve as a
functionalized alkyl source via an alkoxy radical-mediated
selective b-scission, enabling the introduction of a succinimide
fragment into polysubstituted allenes. This method has signif-
icant advantages, including mild reaction conditions, excellent
functional group tolerance, and ease of large-scale synthesis
and product derivatization. Additionally, this cascade can be
extended to the 1,4-alkylazidation of 1,3-enynes. This work not
only enriches the diverse synthesis of functionalized allenes but
also provides a good example of selective C–C bond cleavage in
bicyclic skeletons.

In summary, we have developed a copper-catalyzed 1,4-
alkylcyanation of 1,3-enynes with bicyclic hydroperoxides and
TMSCN. In this cascade, the bicyclic hydroperoxides serve as a
functionalized alkyl source via an alkoxy radical-mediated
selective b-scission, enabling the introduction of a succinimide
fragment into polysubstituted allenes. This method has signif-
icant advantages, including mild reaction conditions, excellent
functional group tolerance, and ease of large-scale synthesis
and product derivatization. Additionally, this cascade can be
extended to the 1,4-alkylazidation of 1,3-enynes. This work not
only enriches the diverse synthesis of functionalized allenes but
also provides a good example of selective C–C bond cleavage in
bicyclic skeletons.
